passages.text:
Five friends, Asha, Bilal, Chen, Dev and Esha, live on floors 1 to 5 of a building, one per floor (floor 1 is the lowest). Each owns a different pet: a cat, a dog, a fish, a parrot or a rabbit.

1. The parrot owner lives on the top floor.
2. Asha lives directly below the rabbit owner.
3. The dog owner lives directly below Esha.
4. Bilal lives on an even-numbered floor.
5. Dev owns neither the cat nor the fish, and lives above Bilal.
6. Chen owns the fish.
7. Chen lives below Asha, and Asha lives below Bilal.

questions.stem: A trader marks goods 50% above cost price. With a discount of d% on the marked price, he still makes a 20% profit. What would his profit or loss be if he gave a discount of 2d% instead?
questions.explanation: 1.5 × (1 − d) = 1.2, so d = 20%. With a 40% discount the selling price is 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9 times cost, a 10% loss. The trap is assuming that doubling the discount halves the profit (giving 10% profit): the discount comes off the marked price, not off the profit.

questions.stem: Two trains start at the same time from towns A and B, 360 km apart, and travel towards each other. After they meet, the train from A takes 4 hours to reach B and the train from B takes 9 hours to reach A. What is the speed of the train from A, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Speed ratio $A : B = \sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} = 3 : 2$, and they meet after $\sqrt{4 \times  9} = 6$ hours. A covers the whole 360 km in 6 + 4 = 10 hours, so 36 km/h (B: $\frac{360}{15} = 24$ km/h; check: 6 × (36 + 24) = 360). Remember: the ratio of speeds is the square root of the inverse ratio of the after-meeting times.

questions.stem: A and B together can finish a job in 12 days. A works alone for 6 days, then B alone finishes the rest in 21 days. How many days would A alone take to do the whole job?
questions.explanation: Let the daily rates be a and b. $a + b = \frac{1}{12}$ and 6a + 21b = 1. From the first equation, $6a + 6b = \frac{1}{2}$, so $15b = \frac{1}{2}$ and $b = \frac{1}{30}$. Then $a = \frac{1}{12} - \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{20}$, so A alone takes 20 days. Add rates (1/days), never the days themselves.

questions.stem: A vessel holds 60 litres of milk. 6 litres are taken out and replaced with water. This is done three times in all. How much milk is left in the vessel?
questions.explanation: Each round keeps $\frac{54}{60} = 0.9$ of the milk, so milk left = $60 \times  0.9^3 = 60 \times  0.729 = 43.74$ litres. 42 litres is the trap: it subtracts 6 litres of milk three times, but after the first round each 6 litres removed is only partly milk.

questions.stem: For how many integer values of k does $x^2 + kx + 36 = 0$ have both roots as integers?
questions.explanation: Integer roots p and q need pq = 36 and k = −(p + q). The positive pairs (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9) and (6,6) give p + q = 37, 20, 15, 13 and 12. The negative pairs give the same sums with a minus sign, so k = ±37, ±20, ±15, ±13, ±12: 10 values. Answering 5 forgets the negative roots.

questions.stem: What is the minimum value of f(x) = |x − 2| + |x − 5| + |x − 9| for real x?
questions.explanation: A sum of distances |x − a| is smallest at the median of the points, here x = 5. f(5) = 3 + 0 + 4 = 7. Trying x = 0 or setting each term to zero separately wastes time; for any odd number of points, go straight to the middle one.

questions.stem: If log₂(log₃(log₄ x)) = 0, what is x?
questions.explanation: Work from the outside in. log₂(y) = 0 means y = 1, so log₃(log₄ x) = 1 and log₄ x = 3. Then $x = 4^3 = 64$. 81 is the trap of stopping at $3^4$ and using the wrong base.

questions.stem: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is $3n^2 + 5n$. What is its 15th term?
questions.explanation: $T_n = S_n - S_{n-1} = (3n^2 + 5n) - (3(n - 1)^2 + 5(n - 1)) = 6n + 2$. So $T_{15} = 92$. Check: T₁ = S₁ = 8 = 6(1) + 2. Substituting n = 15 into Sₙ gives the sum (750), not the term.

questions.stem: What is the remainder when $7^{100}$ is divided by 13?
questions.explanation: 13 is prime, so by Fermat $7^{12}$ leaves remainder 1. 100 = 12 × 8 + 4, so $7^{100}$ leaves the same remainder as $7^4 = 2401$. 2401 = 13 × 184 + 9, so the remainder is 9. Shortcut: $7^2 = 49 \equiv 10 \equiv -3$, so $7^4 \equiv  9$.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, AB = 13, BC = 14 and CA = 15. What is the length of the altitude from A to BC?
questions.explanation: Heron: s = 21, area = $\sqrt{21 \times  8 \times  7 \times  6} = 84$. Altitude to BC = $2 \times  \frac{84}{14} = 12$. Learn 13-14-15 as a known triangle: it is two right triangles (5-12-13 and 9-12-15) joined along the altitude of 12.

questions.stem: Two circles of radius 9 cm and 4 cm touch each other externally. What is the length of their direct common tangent?
questions.explanation: The centres are 9 + 4 = 13 cm apart. Direct tangent = $\sqrt{d^2 - (r_1 - r_2)^2}$ = $\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$ cm. For circles that touch externally this is also $2\sqrt{r_1 r_2} = 2\sqrt{36} = 12$. The transverse formula uses (r₁ + r₂) instead; mixing the two up is the usual mistake.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 6 people sit around a round table if two particular people must not sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: All circular arrangements: (6 − 1)! = 120. With the two together, treat them as one unit: (5 − 1)! × 2 = 48. Not together = 120 − 48 = 72. 48 is the trap: it counts the arrangements you want to exclude.

questions.stem: Who owns the parrot?
questions.explanation: Clue 7 gives Chen < Asha < Bilal, and Bilal is on floor 2 or 4 (clue 4), so Bilal is on 4 and Chen and Asha are on two of floors 1–3. Dev lives above Bilal (clue 5), so Dev is on 5 and owns the parrot (clue 1). Esha then takes the remaining floor among 1–3. Clue 2 puts the rabbit directly above Asha, and clue 3 puts the dog directly below Esha. The only fit is Chen 1, Asha 2, Esha 3: Esha has the rabbit, Asha the dog, Chen the fish (clue 6) and Bilal the cat.

questions.stem: On which floor does Esha live?
questions.explanation: Final grid: 1 Chen (fish), 2 Asha (dog), 3 Esha (rabbit), 4 Bilal (cat), 5 Dev (parrot). Floors 1–3 hold Chen, Asha and Esha, with Chen below Asha. Esha can't be on 1, because no one would be below her to own the dog (clue 3). If Esha were on 2, Asha would be on 3, so the dog (directly below Esha) would be Chen's, but Chen owns the fish. So Esha is on 3.

questions.stem: Which pet does Bilal own?
questions.explanation: Dev has the parrot, Chen the fish, Esha the rabbit and Asha the dog, so Bilal, on floor 4, has the cat. 'Rabbit' is the trap from misreading clue 2 as Bilal being the floor above Asha.

questions.stem: If clue 6 (Chen owns the fish) is removed, how many complete arrangements of floors and pets satisfy the remaining clues?
questions.explanation: Dev stays on 5 with the parrot and Bilal on 4. Case 1: Chen 1, Asha 2, Esha 3. Esha has the rabbit and Asha the dog; Chen and Bilal take the cat and fish in either order: 2 ways. Case 2: Chen 1, Esha 2, Asha 3. Bilal has the rabbit and Chen the dog; Asha and Esha share the cat and fish: 2 ways. Total 4. Removing a clue in CAT usually reopens one swap per case: list the cases, don't redo the whole grid.

questions.stem:
Cities that widen roads to cure congestion often find that, within a few years, traffic is as slow as before. The new capacity lowers the cost of driving at peak hours, so people who used to take the train, travel at another time or skip the trip altogether begin to drive. Economists call this induced demand. The lesson is not that roads are useless, but that in a growing city, adding road space without pricing it mostly reshuffles who sits in the jam.

Which option best captures the essence of the passage?
options: Widening roads in growing cities rarely eases congestion, because the extra capacity draws in new drivers unless road use is priced.
Road widening wastes public money, and cities should invest only in trains.
Economists have shown that no policy can reduce traffic in a growing city.
People switch from trains to cars when roads are widened, which hurts public-transport finances.
questions.explanation: The passage gives a problem (wider roads fill up), a cause (induced demand) and a qualified lesson (unpriced road space just reshuffles the jam). Only the first option keeps all three, including the 'unless priced' condition. B and C overstate the argument ('only', 'no policy'). D picks one detail and adds a claim about finances the passage never makes.

questions.stem:
Early printed books often imitated manuscripts: printers added hand-painted initials, copied scribal abbreviations and cut type to look like handwriting. Readers trusted what looked familiar, so a new technology borrowed the authority of the old one before it developed conventions of its own. Only later did title pages, page numbers and indexes, features native to print, become standard. New media, it seems, first dress up as what they replace.

Which option best captures the essence of the passage?
options: Early print copied the look of manuscripts to win readers' trust and only later developed its own conventions, a pattern new media tend to follow.
Printed books were inferior to manuscripts until title pages and indexes were invented.
Readers in the age of print preferred handwriting and resisted printed books for decades.
Every new technology eventually discards all the features of the one it replaces.
questions.explanation: The core is imitation first, native conventions later, generalised to new media. B invents a quality judgement. C exaggerates 'trusted what looked familiar' into decades of resistance. D swaps the passage's tentative 'it seems... first dress up' for an absolute 'every... discards all'. Summary options that add certainty the author didn't have are wrong.

questions.stem:
Four of these sentences form a coherent paragraph. Which one does not belong?
A. Lighthouses once needed keepers who trimmed wicks and wound clockwork mechanisms through the night.
B. In the twentieth century, automation replaced most of these keepers with timers and electric lamps.
C. Lighthouse towers were often painted in bold stripes so that sailors could tell them apart by day.
D. Today satellite navigation means that many ships rarely look for a lighthouse at all.
E. As a result, some lighthouses have been switched off, and others survive mainly as landmarks.
questions.explanation: A → B → D → E trace a single line: keepers, then automation, then satellites, then lighthouses becoming obsolete ('As a result'). C is about lighthouses but describes their daytime markings, not their declining role. Same subject, different thread: that is how CAT odd-one-out questions are built.

questions.stem:
Arrange the sentences into a coherent paragraph.
A. But the very feature that makes them efficient also makes them fragile.
B. Modern supply chains are built to carry as little inventory as possible.
C. A single delayed shipment can therefore halt an entire production line.
D. Holding less stock frees up cash and cuts storage costs, which is why managers prize this lean design.
questions.explanation: B introduces lean supply chains. D gives the benefit ('this lean design'). A turns it around with 'But the very feature that makes them efficient', which only works once D has shown the efficiency. C's 'therefore' needs A's fragility. In BADC, A's 'efficient' arrives before any benefit has been stated.

notes.text:
CAT DILR sets: arrangements, scheduling, tournaments, tables with missing values.

Approach: (1) Spend the first 4 minutes reading every set and pick the 2–3 with the clearest rules. (2) Draw the grid before reading the questions. (3) Place the fixed clues first (exact positions), then the relative clues, then split into cases. (4) For 'if clue X is removed' questions, keep your cases and reopen only what that clue fixed.

Traps: attempting sets in order; solving one set for 20 minutes.

Free practice: https://logic.puzzlebaron.com/ · https://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/puzzles/

Para summary: choose the option that keeps the paragraph's main claim AND its qualifications.

Approach: (1) In one line, write topic + claim + any 'unless/but'. (2) Remove options that add certainty ('every', 'only', 'no policy'), introduce new claims, or summarise just one example.

Traps: an option that is true to the passage but covers only one detail; an option that repeats the passage's words while changing its claim.

Free practice: summarise one essay a day in a single line. https://aeon.co/essays · https://psyche.co
